Experimental erosion tests were performed on 25.4 x 25.4 x 1.5875 mm Inconel 718 coupons coated with EB-PVD 7YSZ.
The erosion rate, ε, was defined as the ratio of the measured coating erosion mass loss, ΔW, to the mass of impacting particles, Qp.
The maximum erosion rate for the EB-PVD TBC coating occurred at a 90 degree impingement angle, while the maximum for the Inconel 718 substrate occurred between 20-30 degrees.
The erosion rates were found to increase with increased impingement angle, impact velocity, and temperature.
Experimentally-based correlations were developed for TBC erosion rates and particle restitution characteristics as functions of impact velocity, angle, and temperature.
Computational grids were generated using Pointwise V16, with grid clustering near the blade surfaces to achieve y+ < 3.
The three-dimensional flow field solutions used the k-ω Shear-Stress-Transport (SST) turbulence model in ANSYS CFX.
An Euler-Lagrangian two-stage, one-way particle interaction model approach was used for the particle trajectory simulations.
The experimentally-based erosion and restitution models were implemented as user-defined functions in ANSYS CFX.
For the commercial APU turbine, the maximum local TBC erosion rate was predicted to be 72.94 mg/g/cm^2 on the rotor suction side.
The overall blade erosion rates for the commercial APU turbine were predicted to be 0.83 mg/g for the stator and 0.87 mg/g for the rotor.
When particles were only seeded in the 5% of the span near the hub and shroud, the erosion on the stator pressure surface occurred almost exclusively along these thin bands.
The highest erosion rate was still predicted at the shroud and trailing edge corner of the rotor suction surface, where the particles became concentrated due to centrifugal forces.
High-speed photography and particle image displacement velocimetry (PIDV) techniques were used to measure particle restitution characteristics.
The computational simulations were performed for a commercial APU turbine, a NASA designed automotive turbine, and a NASA turbine scaled for modern rotorcraft.
